\[
\mathrm{LBP}_{P,R} = \sum_{p=0}^{P-1} s(g_p - g_c)\, 2^p,
\qquad
s(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & z \ge 0 \\ 0 & z < 0 \end{cases},
\qquad
P = 8,\ R = 1
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(g_c\): The center pixel
- \(g_p\): The sample points on the circle
- \(P, R\): The number of points and the radius

The center pixel is g_c, and g_p are P points on a circle of radius R around it. They start at the right and go counterclockwise. Points between pixels are interpolated. Each point gives a bit: 1 when it is at least as bright as the center. Only the signs of the differences count. So adding a constant to the image or stretching its contrast leaves the codes as they are. The rotation invariant method turns each code to its smallest rotation. Uniform codes have at most two changes between 0 and 1 around the circle. Ojala and coworkers found that they cover most of natural texture. So the uniform method labels them by the number of 1s and puts all others under one label. The variance method gives the variance of the samples instead, a measure of local contrast. The codes are scaled to the full gray range for the image output.
